items.title: Houston Person Part 1 interviewed by Monk Rowe and Michael Woods, Majesty of the Seas, May 29, 1995…
items.q: In the airport they had all jazz, Horace Silver, Miles Davis, John Coltrane.

ctx.x: You know I wanted to ask you to bring that thought home too is you know I find so much beauty in sounds that are produced in the African American community, though they are not in any music method book. You know I’ve never picked up a music method book and have someone tell you how to sing like Aretha Franklin.

Oh, well you won’t find that. No you won’t find that. Well the one thing I can tell you is everywhere I go, I hear American music. Every country in the world, there’ll be some form of American music. I was in Germany last week and I was just amazed, and they were playing some of the R&B and contemporary music, and you know, Barry White and all that, and man I was glad to hear that stuff. I was in a department store and they were just playing, The Manhattans, and Anita Baker, and all these people, then I went in…

items.title: Houston Person Part 2 interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, October 2, 1998 [interview 2 of 2]
items.q: Miles Davis, in his own way, was an entertainer.

ctx.x: Did people, did fellow musicians look askance at that kind of showboating thing?

Well I don’t think so. It was just, to me it was having fun with the music. Because these guys were some of the greatest guys, musicians in the world we’re talking about — Dizzy, Gillespie, who was an entertainer. The greatest jazz musician of all, Louis Armstrong, was an entertainer. Lionel Hampton was an entertainer. See that element got lost somewhere. Miles Davis, in his own way, was an entertainer. All these guys. Mingus. You know, you look back you trace all the great guys, they were entertainers. Illinois…
